opener.heading: Week 45: On the Farm 🚜
about: On Friday you tape a farm onto the living room floor and it stays there until Thursday. She gets fields, a track and a muddy yard, and every toy animal in the house moves in. The days after that hang something new on the same farm: a cardboard cow with a glove for an udder, a pig in a wig, three houses for the wolf to blow down, five animals wearing her name on card tags. Print runs under all of it. The five letters of her name, the sound at the front of a word and the big word on a milk carton each arrive attached to something she built herself.

Thursday is Veterans Day. Shearing day runs as written, the farm gets packed into a box that afternoon, and the walk out to the shed passes whatever flags are up on your street. Stop at one and tell her whose day it is. A minute covers it, and she will ask again next year.
azlyn: The five letters of her name. A, Z, L, Y, N on a gate sign, on five ear tags, drawn in salt and called out at the gate.
The sound at the front of a word. She sorts animals and kitchen objects onto three towels by how each word starts.
Rhyming pairs. Pig and wig, hen and pen, goat and coat, matched by ear and then built out of the toys she owns.
Print does a job. She reads the big word off the milk, the oats and the flour, then stands the real food under each one.
Cutting, gluing and threading through five ear tags, five woolly sheep and a bag of fleece she shears herself.
you: Her own name is the doorway and it doesn't generalize for a while
Tracing in salt removes the fear of getting it wrong
Hearing a rhyme and making one are two different skills, months apart
The first sound in a word is the easiest one to hear, and that's where reading starts
Twenty-six is too many, and five is plenty
Print in the real world teaches more than print in a book
Repetition of one sound all day does more than a lesson on it

opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 17 months this week. He kicks a ball and carries things while he walks, and two-word combinations are starting. He turns 17 months on Friday the 5th.

days.title: The Farm on the Floor
days.prepTonight: Pull six or eight boxes and tubs out of the recycling into the living room, with the masking tape, the brown kraft paper and the marker on top.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Farm Book From the Shelf

opening.title: Every Animal in the House
opening.need: 1 laundry basket · every toy animal in the house · 4 dish towels.
steps: Send her round the house with the basket. Every animal she finds comes back in it, farm or not.
Tip the lot on the living room floor. Four dish towels out, and she sorts them: the ones that live on a farm and the ones that don't.
Split the farm pile again by who lives with who. Leave the piles where she puts them. You build the fields round them at 9:15.

main.title: Fields, Pens and a Track
materials: 6–8 cardboard boxes and tubs in mixed sizes
1 sheet brown kraft paper, or a flattened box, for the muddy yard
Every toy animal in the house
steps: Lay the track first. Two lines of masking tape down the middle of the room, wide enough for her to walk between.
Tape out a field for each pile she made at 8:00, on the side she left it. Follow her layout even where it wastes half the floor.
Cut two boxes down to ankle height so she can lift animals in over the wall. She stands back while you cut, and says where the gate goes.
Stand the tubs and small boxes as the barn and the shed. She chooses which is which.
Tape the brown paper flat at the end of the track for the muddy yard. She draws the puddles and the trough onto it in marker.
Now she moves every animal in. A cow in the duck pen is her decision and it stands.
main.tip: Tape to the floor rather than the rug. The farm has to last until Thursday, and low-tack masking tape lifts off floorboards clean.

outside.title: The Plowed Field
paras: Walk to a plowed field, or the biggest bare patch of ground within reach. November leaves it in ridges and troughs, and the clay comes home on her boots. Walk the edge, never the middle. Count the furrows out loud, and let her stand in one to see how deep it comes.

days.infant: Kreston turns 17 months today. He kicks a ball now, and he will walk the taped track end to end. Give him the biggest animal in the house, too big for his mouth, and a tub of his own at the yard end. Two-word combinations are starting, so expect cow gone the first time he posts one behind the sofa.

second.title: Naming the Farm
second.intro: The farm has fields, a track and a muddy yard and no name. She fixes that this afternoon.
materials: Thick card or cereal boxes, 6–8 pieces
Crayons, or washable paint and a brush
2 small boxes, to prop the gate
Your phone, for the before photo
steps: Ask her what the farm is called and write it down word for word, however long it runs.
Write the name across the shoebox lid in marker, big, then AZLYN underneath it, saying each letter as you make it. She colors the rest.
Stand the lid on its edge across the gateway as the gate, and prop it there with a box behind each corner.
Then the cards. She names each field and pen, you write her words down, she decorates.
Tape a craft stick to the back of every sign and tape the stick down inside its field so it stands up.
Walk her round and let her read every sign back.
Photograph the farm from the doorway with the gate in shot. Thursday needs the before picture.
second.tip: Write her words down as she says them. The cows that are brown beats Brown Field, and she will correct you if you tidy it.

alternatives: One sign over the gate and nothing else.
Draw the farm from above on a big sheet of paper.
Line the animals up by size and name the biggest.
Paint the boxes and name the farm tomorrow.
outAgain: Grandparents, or whoever is nearest, and she takes a field card to show them
The park while the light holds, because it is gone before six
A friend's house, if the farm survives an hour alone
The corner store for tomorrow's milk
A drive past the fields you walked this morning

aroundWorld.title: Milk, Everywhere 🥛
paras: Cows are one option out of many. Mongolian families milk mares and ferment it into airag, poured for guests all summer. Across the Himalayas the milk comes from yaks and goes into salty butter tea. India produces more milk than any other country, and much of it comes from water buffalo, thicker and sweeter than a cow's.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Half fill a jam jar with heavy cream, screw the lid down tight and let her shake it. It goes to whipped cream, then grainy, then a lump of butter drops out of the buttermilk. Ten minutes, and it goes on toast.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Reindeer milk is the richest of the lot, around five times the fat of cow's milk.

days.krestonPM: Kreston is 17 months and copies whatever hands are doing at the table. Give him card and a crayon while Azlyn makes her signs, and tape his up in the yard. He will reach for the marker, so keep it out of range.

insight.headline: Her own name is the doorway and it doesn't generalize for a while.
paras: Azlyn knows her name on sight long before she knows a single letter, because she reads the whole shape of it the way she reads a road sign. The A at the front of AZLYN belongs to her name and stays there for months. The A in APPLE is a separate problem, and there is nothing wrong with her when she doesn't see it. So the sign over the gate earns its hour. She has a word she cares about, she watched you build it out of parts, and saying those letters in order hands her five keys she will use on every other word.

days.safety: Small plastic farm animals are choke-size for Kreston at 17 months, and the whole farm sits at his height. Gate the room, shut the door or move the build onto a table the moment he is loose in there. Nothing gets strung across the gateway at any point this week, because a line at his neck height is a strangulation risk for both of them. The lid stands on its own edge instead, and it goes flat on the floor the moment either of them pushes it. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: The Cardboard Cow
days.prepTonight: Stand the biggest box you have by the kitchen door with two old towels, the gloves and the bucket, and write AZLYN big on a card.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Two Boot Prints Side by Side

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Tray You Can Rub Out

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Warm Bath After the Wet Morning

opening.title: Four Fingers and a Pin
opening.need: 1 dishwashing glove · 1 straight pin (adult only) · warm water · the sink.
steps: Fill the glove at the tap, hold the wrist shut in your fist and hand it to her two-handed. It has fingers and it is heavy.
Hold it over the sink and prick one fingertip with the pin. Her hands stay behind her back. One hole, one thin jet.
Prick the other three and let her squeeze them out. The cow arrives at 9:15. Put the pin out of reach.

main.title: Milking the Glove
materials: 1 straight pin or a needle (adult only)
1 large cardboard box for the cow
Packing tape and a permanent marker
steps: Towels down first, one under the working spot and one folded by the door.
Build the cow. Box on its side, flaps taped shut with packing tape, a face on one end in marker. She picks the head end.
Fill a glove with warm water, tested on the inside of your wrist. Twist the wrist end over and tape it shut hard.
Prick four fingertips once each with the pin over the sink, because a cow has four teats. Leave the thumb. Tape the glove under the box so all four fingers hang at her sitting height.
Stool under the cow, bucket under the glove, her on the stool. Show her the grip once: thumb and finger closed at the top, then squeeze down. Pulling gets nothing.
Refill and run it again. Three gloves is a morning's milking, and the last one can have eight holes.
main.tip: She will try to hold the bucket and milk at the same time. Let her, and let it go over once.

outside.title: Two Boot Prints Side by Side
paras: Find the softest ground within reach, at a field gate or the edge of a path that has not drained since Tuesday. She presses one boot in hard and lifts it straight up for a clean print. Put yours beside hers. Then hunt the same stretch for prints neither of you made: dog, bird, hoof.

days.infant: Kreston is 17 months and walks well enough to stamp on purpose. Put him down in the same patch, take his hand and lift him off his print so he can look at it. He will go back and flatten it. A bootful of mud is a fine reason for his first two-word sentence.

second.title: The Tray You Can Rub Out
second.intro: The salt tray is the calmest thing in this book. Clear the table and set it up while she watches.
materials: 1 baking sheet or roasting pan with a lip
Fine salt, 2 cups (fine semolina or all-purpose flour works the same)
Dark card or foil to line the tray
1 chopstick, or the wrong end of a paintbrush
Her name written big on a card
steps: Line the tray with the dark card, or foil shiny side up, so her lines show black.
Pour the salt in and let her level it with the flat of her hand. As deep as a fingernail. Any deeper and the lines close behind her finger.
Stand the name card at the top of the tray. She copies the first letter with one finger, straight into the salt.
Shake the tray flat. Do it again. She can run it thirty times.
Hand her the chopstick when her finger tires. It draws thinner and slower.
Lay the animal cards along the edge and let her draw those too.
Leave the tray set up. She comes back to it at 4:15 on her own.
second.tip: Say nothing about backwards letters. A backwards Z at three is standard and mileage fixes it. Correct it now and you teach her the tray is a test.

alternatives: Flour on a dark baking sheet, if the salt is spoken for.
Draw in the condensation on the kitchen window.
Shaving foam spread flat on the tray, messier.
Her name in wet sand, or in this morning's mud.
outAgain: The museum, first Saturday of the month, hunting anything with an animal on it
The farm stand or the market, if the museum is packed
The park, and let her get cold before dinner
A café with a window and something to watch
The library, a few days early, for a farm book
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 17 months and a museum is one long corridor to run down. Let him walk stretches on his own feet and carry him past anything at grabbing height. He points and waits for the word, so give him one word per point.

insight.headline: Tracing in salt removes the fear of getting it wrong.
paras: Hand a three-year-old a pencil and paper and the mistake stays on the page in front of her. Azlyn knows that, and a fair share of the wobble in early writing comes from a child who has decided she cannot do it. Salt has no memory. She draws an A, it comes out backwards, she shakes the tray and the A is gone. She has nothing to rub out and nobody to show it to. Her finger in salt feeds her more than a pencil does, the drag and the grain arriving through her skin. Fifteen attempts in salt cost her nothing.

days.safety: The pin is yours. Make every hole yourself and count it back into your hand at the end. Warm water, never hot, tested on your wrist. A bucket with water in it is a drowning risk for a 17-month-old, so it never sits on the floor unattended and it gets emptied when the milking stops. Keep the second towel down; the wet floor is a slip risk for everyone. Two cups of loose salt is a poisoning risk swallowed, so the tray works at the far end of the table with Kreston in the high chair, and the salt goes back in its box and up out of reach when the 4:15 quiet play ends, the tray staying at the far end of the table until then.

days.title: The Pig in a Wig
days.prepTonight: Put the wool scraps, an odd sock, a small box and a toy truck on the table, and start a grocery bag of shredded junk mail for tomorrow.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Rhyme Pairs on the Rug

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Last Song of the Day

opening.title: Which Two Sound the Same
opening.need: 1 basket · four things that rhyme with an animal (a wig of wool, a sock to be the coat, a small box to be the pen, a toy truck).
steps: Say two words at the table and ask her if the ends match. Pig and wig. Cow and cat. Hen and pen. Keep going until she calls the wrong ones before you finish.
Hand her the basket and send her for the four things, one at a time, naming each as it goes in. The sock is a coat now and the box is a pen.
Line them along the table and say the animal that belongs to each. Pig, goat, hen, duck. Leave the line there. It is the shopping list for 9:15, and the sheep needs nothing but somewhere to sleep.

main.title: The Pig in a Wig
materials: Toy animals, or animals drawn on card and cut out
Wool scraps or cotton balls for the wig
1 sock or a fabric offcut for the coat
1 toy truck, or a box on a string
steps: Start with the pig. Tape wool scraps over its head until it has a proper wig, and let her say how much is enough.
The goat gets the coat. Sock over the body, head out of the top, and she does the pulling.
The hen gets a pen. Box on its side, hen in, and write PEN on the front in marker while she watches each letter arrive.
The duck gets the truck. She loads it and drives it the length of the room, saying both words every trip.
The sheep goes to sleep. On its side, everybody whispering, and it stays asleep all day.
Say the whole list back in order, pointing at each. Then ask her for a daft pair of her own. A cow in a plow, a rat in a hat, build whatever she offers.
main.tip: Land on the ends of the words. Pig and wig do not sound the same at the front, and that is the part she has to learn to stop listening to.

outside.title: Splashing Down the Muddy Lane
paras: Rain boots, the muddiest lane you know, and no destination. Every puddle gets stood in. Run the rhyme game as you walk, one pair per puddle, and let her call them out over the splashing. The clocks went back last night, so the light under the hedges is going by half past four now. Go while the light is high.

days.infant: Kreston is 17 months and a puddle is the best thing in his week. Hold one hand and let him stamp in the shallow end of the same puddle Azlyn is in. He kicks a ball now, and he kicks water the same way, sideways with the whole leg. Bring a full change of clothes.

second.title: The Barn Dance
second.intro: She has the moves, the music and the caller's job. Push the sofa back and take the rug up before anybody puts boots on.
materials: Music on a speaker or a phone
1 scarf or a dish towel each
Rain boots or boots, indoors, on purpose
steps: Ask her for four dance moves. Stamp, spin, clap, jump, whatever comes. Draw each one on a card in marker while she names it.
Boots on indoors. She will not believe you at first.
Music on, four cards in her hand. She is the caller. She holds one up, shouts it, and the room does it until she holds up the next.
Give two people the wooden spoons to bang the beat on the floor, and swap them halfway through.
A scarf or a dish towel each. Swing them overhead on the spins, and let go on purpose once.
Lay the broom flat on the floor. Dance up one side and down the other without touching it, then hop over it on the beat.
Last dance slow, big light off, everybody swaying. She calls that one too.
second.tip: Take her calls even when they come three seconds apart and nobody can keep up. Being obeyed by a room full of adults is the whole appeal.

alternatives: Two moves instead of four, and the spoons only.
One song, then the rhyming book on the sofa.
Musical statues with the same four cards.
One real square-dance move, taught and left there.
outAgain: Scooter or balance bike down the flattest stretch you have, hat and gloves on
The park, for the swings while they are dry
A long loop with the stroller to walk off the barn dance
Feeding the ducks, who are hungry by November
A drive out to see cows or sheep, counted from the car
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 17 months and this is his kind of afternoon. Give him one wooden spoon and let him bang whatever he chooses. Hold both his hands for the spins. Two-word combinations are starting, so name each move before it happens and see which one he gives back.

insight.headline: Hearing a rhyme and making one are two different skills, months apart.
paras: Azlyn will tell you that pig and wig sound the same long before she can hand you a word that rhymes with hat. Spotting a rhyme is a matching job and she is good at it now. Making one asks her to hold an ending still in her head, run through everything she knows and test each word against it, and that arrives later on its own schedule. Give her the pairs ready-made and let her hear a few hundred of them. The night she offers you pig, wig, big, zig out of nowhere in the bath, she has crossed over on the strength of the hundreds.

days.safety: Boots slide on bare boards with the rug up, so check the floor is dry before the music goes on, and nobody dances in socks. The broom stays flat on the floor and nobody stands on the handle, which rolls underfoot. Scarves get let go upward and never at a face. Kreston is at knee height to everyone dancing, so he is in your arms or holding both your hands the whole time the floor is stamping, and out of the room with the door shut if nobody has a hand free for him.

days.title: C is for Cow
days.prepTonight: Tear a grocery bag of junk mail into shreds for the afternoon, draw a wolf on a piece of card and leave it face down on the table.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Sticks for the Second Little Pig

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Two Books and the Small Lamp

opening.title: Sorting the Herd
steps: Carry the animals to the table in the basket, tip them out in the middle and ask her for two piles. Any rule she likes, and she does not have to tell you first.
Ask what the rule was. Take the answer as it comes, including these ones are the good ones.
Sort again by a different rule, then leave them out. At 9:15 you hand her a rule she has never met.

main.title: Everything That Starts Like Cow
materials: Ordinary objects from around the house, 10–15: a cup, a spoon, a pan, a saucer, a clothespin, a sock, a corn cob
1 basket or a tray to carry the finds in
steps: Lay the three dish towels out with a gap between them. Write c, s and p on the three cards and stand one on each towel.
Say cow, stretching the front of it until it is silly, and ask what she hears at the start. Put the cow on the c towel.
Do sheep and pig the same way, one onto each of the other towels.
Hand her the basket and let her post the rest, animal by animal and object by object. Cup, spoon, clothespin, corn, sock, pan, saucer. Say every word out loud first.
Leave the wrong ones where she puts them. Say the word again, stretched, and let her move it herself if she hears it.
Count each towel at the end and let her say the winning sound five times, as loud as she likes.
main.tip: Say the sound, not the letter name. c as in cow, a short click at the front, never see. Letter names are the part she would have to unlearn.

outside.title: Sticks for the Second Little Pig
paras: Take a bag and fill it with twigs, the thin dropped ones that come off the hedges in the first proper wind of November. Anything longer than her forearm is too long, so snap it or leave it. She will collect forty and you need fifteen. Hunt the s words as you go: stick, stone, sign.

days.infant: Kreston is 17 months and carries things while he walks now. Give him his own bag and let him fill it with whatever he judges suitable, leaves included. He hands things over one at a time to whoever will take them, so take everything and say the word.

second.title: Straw, Sticks and Bricks
second.intro: Three houses go up on the floor this afternoon, and she knows how the story ends.
materials: Shredded junk mail, dry grass or straw
3 toy pigs, or pigs drawn on card
steps: Tape three squares on the floor, well apart. One house per square, and she picks which square gets which material.
House one is the shredded paper, heaped up and patted into walls. It will not stand.
House two is the twigs, leaned into a tent shape and taped where two of them cross at the top.
House three is the boxes, stacked into walls with a flat one across for a roof. Ask which she would live in before anything gets tested.
A pig in each house. Then turn the wolf card over and stand him at the far end of the room.
She huffs at house one and it goes everywhere. House two comes down in a heap. House three holds, and she can push it as hard as she likes.
Rebuild whichever one she asks for and run it again. She will pick the straw house.
second.tip: Let her be the wolf. Doing the huffing herself puts her in charge of the frightening part.

alternatives: Two houses instead of three, straw and bricks.
Build them outside from what is in the yard.
Act it out with her under a blanket as the house.
Draw the three houses on one long sheet of paper.
outAgain: The playground with the big slide, wrapped up, and check the slide is dry
The woods loop, for more sticks and better ones
The riverside path, to see how high the water is
A green space and a ball, if the wolf left her any energy
Home early with the lamps on, because it is dark by five
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 17 months and he will flatten all three houses before she has finished the first. Build him a fourth square at the far end of the room out of the boxes alone, and let him knock it down as often as he wants. Keep the shredded paper at her end of the room.

insight.headline: The first sound in a word is the easiest one to hear, and that's where reading starts.
paras: Pulling a whole word apart into its separate sounds is heavy work for a three-year-old, and Azlyn is nowhere near it. The front of a word is a different story. Say cow and the c comes off in her hand, because her mouth starts there and it is the part she can feel herself making. Children who can hear the first sound in a spoken word go on to read sooner than children who can't, and it is one of the strongest early signals there is. The dish towels teach her that words are made of pieces, and everything else sits on that. The alphabet can wait.

days.safety: Twigs carried at running speed sit at eye height for both children, so sticks stay in the three squares and nobody runs with one. Kreston will put dry grass and shredded paper straight in his mouth at 17 months. Sweep the floor before he is put down, and keep the shredded bag out of reach while he is loose.

days.title: Marking the Herd
days.prepTonight: Put the cereal box, the hole punch and five short lengths of wool on the table, and wash six empty packets for tomorrow: milk, oats, flour, eggs, rice, tea.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Tagged Animals in a Line

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Wet Hair and the Animal Book

opening.title: Which Five Animals
opening.need: the animals off the floor farm · 1 basket · the name card from Saturday.
steps: Tell her five of the animals are about to become hers, with her name on them, and she picks which five.
She chooses. Do not steer her towards the good ones. Three ducks and a broken horse is a fine herd.
Stand the name card up and count the letters with her. Five letters, five animals, one each. Carry them to the table in the basket.

main.title: The Five Ear Tags
materials: Thick card, or a cereal box
1 hole punch, or a sharp pencil and a lump of modeling clay to push into
steps: Cut five tags out of the cereal box, each about the size of a stamp. You cut, she counts them out loud as they come off.
She colors all five, front and back, however she wants.
Write one letter of her name on each tag in marker, in order, saying it as you make it. A. Z. L. Y. N.
Punch a hole in the corner of each, or push the pencil through onto the modeling clay. Let her point at where the hole goes.
Thread a length of wool through each hole and tie it round an animal's leg. Tie it short, cut the tails off, leave nothing that makes a loop.
Stand the five in a line in name order and read them left to right. Then muddle them and let her put them back.
main.tip: Give her the letters in her own order if that is what she wants. The sequence comes this afternoon at the gate.

outside.title: Frost on the Gate
paras: The first real frost is about due. Go out early to catch it where the sun has not reached, on the north side of walls and along the top bar of a metal gate. Put her bare hand flat on the gate for two seconds and take it off again. Breathe out and watch it. Find a puddle with a skin of ice and let her put a boot through it.

days.infant: Kreston is 17 months and has had almost no cold in his life yet. Hold his hand against the frosted gate bar for a second, take it straight off and give him the word for it. He will ask again by reaching. Mittens back on, and that is the whole of it, one touch each.

second.title: Roll Call at the Gate
second.intro: Five animals are wearing her name and all five are about to go missing. She works the gate this afternoon with a clipboard.
materials: 1 piece of stiff card and a binder clip, or a real clipboard
The shoebox lid gate from Friday
steps: Make the clipboard together: stiff card, the paper on top, binder clip across the short edge.
Draw five boxes down the sheet in marker and write a letter of her name beside each, the same five as this morning.
She shuts her eyes and counts to ten at the gate while you hide the five round the room. Behind a cushion, under a chair.
Stand the lid gate on its edge across the gateway. Nothing comes onto the farm until she calls it in.
She hunts. Every animal she finds comes back to the gate, she finds its letter, ticks the box in marker, and only then does the gate tip open.
Call the register at the end. A. Z. L. Y. N. An empty box means somebody is still out in the dark, and she goes back for it.
Count the five into a pen and shut the gate on them for the night.
second.tip: Say the letter every time an animal goes through the gate. She will hear each of the five twenty times this afternoon.

alternatives: Hide two animals instead of five and skip the clipboard.
Hide them in the yard and do the roll call at the back door.
She hides them and you do the ticking.
Tag the family instead, one card each, register at dinner.
outAgain: Swimming, and she floats on her back longer than she could in September
Indoor playground, if the pool is closed for a school session
The library, a day early, for a book about sheep
A warm café and a window, if nobody has it in them
The indoor play center
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 17 months and swimming looks different now that he walks. He wants the steps at the shallow end, going in and out on his own feet, so let him with a hand on him. Keep it to twenty-five minutes and get him dressed before he goes cold.

insight.headline: Twenty-six is too many, and five is plenty.
paras: An alphabet frieze on the wall hands Azlyn twenty-six shapes with nothing to attach them to, and she learns the song without learning a letter. Five is a different proposition. Her five come with a reason: they are her name, they are on her animals, and she put them there. Children learn the letters in their own name first and hold onto them, because the word carries a meaning worth the effort of remembering. Get those five solid, the shape and the sound both, and the other twenty-one arrive across the next year without a single drill from either of you.

days.safety: Loops of wool or string tied round toys are a strangulation risk for Kreston at 17 months. Tie every tag short, cut the tails off, and count the five animals out and the five back in before he goes down in that room. The scissors and the hole punch stay with you. On the gate, bare skin comes off frozen metal after a count of two, both children, and wet or damp hands do not go on the bar at all. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: Reading the Packets
days.prepTonight: Stand the six rinsed packets on the counter with the string, the clothespins and the scissors, and check there are cotton balls in the house for tomorrow.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Everything That Came Off a Farm

opening.title: Everything That Came Off a Farm
opening.need: 1 tray · the fridge and one cupboard shelf.
steps: Open the fridge and let her take out everything that started on a farm. You hold the door and carry the heavy ones.
Line it all up on the tray. Butter, eggs, cheese, milk, a carrot, the bacon. Then the cupboard shelf, for the flour, the oats and the honey.
Ask which animal or which plant each one came off. Correct nothing yet. Leave the tray out; the afternoon needs the milk.

main.title: The Words Off the Packets
materials: 6 empty packets and cartons: milk, oats, flour, eggs, rice, tea
The real food from the cupboard
steps: Tie the string between the front legs of two dining chairs, down at her knee height, tight enough to hold what hangs on it.
Cut the big word off the front of each packet. You cut. She points at which word is the big one.
Spread the six pieces face up. Read each one out, running your finger under the word left to right as you say it.
Turn each piece over and write the same word on the back in plain capitals, so she can flip it and see the word without the picture.
She clips all six on the line, picture side out, one clothespin each and two for the stiff ones.
Now the food. She fetches the real milk, oats and flour and stands each under its word. Read the wrong ones again and let her move them herself.
main.tip: She is reading the colors and the picture, and that is how everybody starts. Turning the piece over to the plain capitals shows her there is something underneath the picture.

outside.title: Six Signs Before the Corner
paras: Walk to the corner and count six pieces of writing on the way. A stop sign, a street name, a house number, the store sign, a poster in a window, the word on a van. Read each one out and say what it is doing there. Six before the corner, six different ones coming back.

days.infant: Kreston is 17 months and points at things and waits for you to name them. Point at the red stop sign and give him stop. He will point at the next one himself, and he may give you the sign and the van in one breath.

second.title: Curds and Whey
second.intro: A quart of milk, a squeeze of lemon and a strainer, and she watches milk come apart into two things with two names. Cheese on bread by five thirty.
materials: Lemon juice or white vinegar, 3 tbsp
1 clean dish towel or a square of cheesecloth
1 small pot with a lid, and a label she writes
steps: Pour the milk into the saucepan and heat it until it steams and the first bubbles come up round the edge. She watches sitting down, and the pan handle points inward.
Off the heat. Stir in three tablespoons of lemon juice, one at a time, and let her count them in.
Leave it ten minutes. It comes apart into white lumps and cloudy liquid, and the two have names: curds and whey.
Sit the strainer over the bowl, line it with the dish towel, and pour the pan through with her standing well back.
Once it is cool enough for her hands, she gathers the corners of the towel and squeezes the whey out.
Salt it, taste it, salt it again. She decides when it is right, and she will over-salt it once.
Pack it into the pot. She writes her label with the marker and presses it on, then spreads a cracker each and everybody eats one before the pot goes in the fridge.
second.tip: Keep the whey in the bowl and let her look at it after. A quart of milk in and a fistful of cheese out raises the obvious question.

alternatives: Shake cream into butter in a jam jar. No stovetop.
Yogurt and honey stirred together, and skip the heat.
Read six packets in the cupboard without cutting anything.
Clip the words up and hang the laundry beside them.
outAgain: The library, and she asks at the desk for a book about farms herself
Indoor playground, if the library is full of the after-school crowd
The park on the way home while there is light in it
The store for tomorrow's bread, and she reads the sign
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 17 months and the board book corner is his half of the library. He will pull six off the shelf and read none of them. Let Azlyn choose his book and carry it to the desk.

insight.headline: Print in the real world teaches more than print in a book.
paras: Azlyn sees the word on the milk carton every morning of her life, in her hands, attached to something she drinks. That word has a job. The same word in a picture book sits in a row of others with nothing riding on it. Children start reading with the print that is doing something in their world: the store sign, the cereal box, the front of a bus. Reading the packets puts her in front of print with a purpose, and the shopping shelf becomes something the two of you can work on for two years without calling it a lesson.

days.safety: A pan of milk at near boiling and a bowl of hot whey are the two hazards this afternoon. She stays sitting at the table until the pan is off the heat, the pan handle turns inward throughout, and nothing hot comes down to floor level while Kreston is walking about. The word line runs at knee height between the chair legs and never at neck height, and it comes down and goes away the moment the six words come off it. The sign hunt ends at a corner, so hold Kreston's hand from the curb onward, keep yourself between both children and the road, and read every sign from the sidewalk. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: Shearing Day
days.prepTonight: Cut five sheep shapes out of cereal boxes after she is in bed, stand them by the cotton balls and the glue, and find a big box with a lid.

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: The Forks, Last Time This Week

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Farm Photos From the Week

opening.title: Sticking the Wool On
opening.need: the five sheep shapes · 1 bag of cotton balls · 1 glue stick.
steps: Count the cotton balls out of the bag onto the table with her, and remember the number.
She glues them over the five sheep until no card shows through. A thin sheep is no fun to shear.
Stand them on the windowsill to dry. Say shhheep and shhhears with the front stretched, and tell her shearing starts at 9:15.

main.title: Shearing Day
materials: 5 sheep shapes cut from cereal boxes
Cotton balls, 1 bag (torn paper towels or old cushion stuffing works too)
1 glue stick, or white school glue and a brush
steps: Check the glue is dry. Any bald patch gets one more cotton ball, glued or brushed on.
Hand her the safety scissors and start with sheep one. She cuts the wool off close to the card, and every scrap goes in the paper bag.
Number the back of each sheep 1 to 5 in marker as it comes off.
Shear the rest. It takes longer than you expect, her hand will ache, and she will not want help.
Weigh the fleece by hand. Her hands, then yours. Heavy and light, both words, out loud.
Write FLEECE on the paper bag, let her say each letter as it goes on, then tape it shut and put it with the farm.
main.tip: Safety scissors are hard work for a three-year-old and this is a lot of cutting. Let her stop at three sheep.

outside.title: The Shed in November
paras: Take her out to the shed, the garage or the trash bins and open it up. Look at what is put away for winter: the hose, the folded chairs, the empty pots. Name everything with sh at the front, starting with the shed. Today is Veterans Day, so stop at any flag on the way back and say whose day it is.

days.infant: Kreston is 17 months and a shed is head height in hazards, so keep him at the door and hand things out rather than letting him in. He carries while he walks now, so give him the empty pot to take up the path, and he will kick it along like a ball.

second.title: Putting the Farm to Bed
second.intro: The farm has been on the living room floor since Friday and it shuts down for winter this afternoon.
materials: The floor farm, the signs and the tagged animals
The sheared sheep and the bag of fleece
Shredded paper, or the leftover fleece, for bedding
steps: Walk the farm one last time and read every sign out, field by field. Let her tell you who lived where.
Bring the animals in off the fields, biggest first, down the track and through the gate. She counts them as they come.
Bed the box. Shredded paper or leftover fleece in the bottom, dish towels folded over the top as blankets.
Big light off, flashlight on. She checks every pen with the beam and says goodnight to whoever is in it.
Untie the five wool tags and drop them in with the animals, so nothing goes into storage wearing a loop.
The sheared sheep and the bag of fleece go in last, on top. Then the signs, flat, and the shoebox lid gate.
Peel the masking tape up off the floor together. It comes away in long strips. Write the farm's name and the date on the lid.
second.tip: Tell her it comes back out. A box packed and waiting on top of the closet is a farm she can ask for on a wet Tuesday in January.

alternatives: Pack the animals and leave the tape down for the weekend.
Photograph every sign before it comes down.
Move the farm onto a tray so it survives on a shelf.
Skip the packing and play in it one last time.
outAgain: The garden center, warm, bright and full of things put to bed for winter
The farm stand, for eggs and a look out the back
The park before it goes dark, coat zipped to the chin
The hardware store, for a bigger box and a bag of bulbs
A drive to see Friday's fields, plowed and empty
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 17 months and copies chores now, so hand him one animal at a time and let him post it into the box. He takes two back out for every three that go in. Give him the flashlight at the end and let him see his own hand lit from underneath.

insight.headline: Repetition of one sound all day does more than a lesson on it.
paras: Azlyn has had sh a dozen times today without once sitting down to learn it: sheep, shears, shed, shelf, shut, and you shushing her at the shed door. That is how a sound goes in. A three-year-old needs it to turn up again and again across different words, in her hands and in her mouth and inside something she cares about, before she can hear it on its own. Ten minutes of drilling one sound at a table buys you compliance. Sixty of them spread across a day she enjoyed buy you the sound, and she never noticed it happening.

days.safety: Cotton balls are the wrong size in the worst way for a 17-month-old, and Kreston will have one in his mouth inside a minute. None of them go to him at any point today, the bag stays up on the table between sheep, and the work happens with him in the high chair or out of the room. Count them out of the bag at 8:00 and count the scraps into the paper bag at the end. The safety scissors stay on the table between sheep, and check the floor before he is put down near it.
